**Monday, February 29, 1960**

February 29 comes around only once every four years, which means its anniversaries are few enough to catalog. By 1960, the date had accumulated a small but striking collection of prior moments.

On **February 29, 1692**, colonial magistrates in Massachusetts issued the first arrest warrants of the Salem witch trials, naming Sarah Good, Sarah Osborne, and Tituba. Nineteen people would eventually be executed. A society consuming itself through accusation and fear became one of early America's defining cautionary tales — and one of its most durable ones.

On **February 29, 1940** — the February 29 immediately before your birth, exactly twenty years prior — Hattie McDaniel became the first African American to win an Academy Award. She was escorted to a segregated table at the back of the Coconut Grove ballroom, separated from the white stars of *Gone with the Wind*. She won Best Supporting Actress and gave a gracious speech. The people who placed her at that separate table believed they were maintaining a permanent order. The child born twenty years later would spend her life watching that order dismantle.

The world you arrived in on February 29, 1960, was already in the middle of that dismantling. **Twenty-eight days before your birth**, four Black students sat at a Woolworth's lunch counter in Greensboro, North Carolina, and refused to leave when denied service. By the time you were born, the sit-in movement had spread to dozens of cities across the South. The civil rights revolution was no longer a coming thing — it had arrived. The February 29 child drew first breath in the middle of it.

On the night of your birth — at roughly 11:47 PM local time in Morocco — the port city of Agadir was struck by an earthquake. The shaking lasted fifteen seconds. The old medina collapsed. Between 12,000 and 15,000 people died — more than a third of the city's entire population. Agadir was rebuilt from scratch, on new ground, away from the site of the old city entirely. The city that exists today bears the same name as the one destroyed on the day you were born; it was built entirely afterward, as if starting over.

Now consider what happened on **February 29, 2020** — your sixtieth birthday.

The United States recorded its first confirmed death from COVID-19 that day: a resident of a nursing home in Kirkland, Washington. The date was February 29, 2020. Within two weeks, the NBA suspended its season, Broadway went dark, and the country began shutting down in ways it had not experienced since the Second World War. You turned sixty on the day the pandemic announced itself in America. It was, in retrospect, the last February 29 before the world changed — or more precisely, the day the change made its first American entry.

Step back and consider 1960 itself. It was the year seventeen African nations gained independence — Nigeria, Senegal, Congo, and more — the colonial map of Africa dissolving faster than anyone had predicted. It was the year Kennedy and Nixon held the first televised presidential debates. It was the year a U-2 spy plane piloted by Francis Gary Powers was shot down over the Soviet Union, destroying the Paris summit and demonstrating that the Cold War extended to the stratosphere. The world of your birth was reorganizing itself in every direction simultaneously.

You were born two and a half years after Sputnik, one year before Yuri Gagarin, nine years before the Moon landing. In 66 years: the Moon at age 9; Nixon's fall at 14; the personal computer through your twenties; the Berlin Wall at 29; the Soviet Union's collapse at 31; the internet remaking everything through your thirties and forties; 9/11 at 41; the smartphone at 47; a pandemic announced on your sixtieth birthday; and now, at 66, an AI revolution that is changing what it means to write, to think, and to know things.

The leap day child has 66 years of life and only 16 actual February 29 birthdays. The next arrives in 2028. The date's rarity means the world's transformations mostly arrive on other days — ordinary February 28ths and March 1sts. But when the date itself has appeared, it has not appeared quietly: a city founded on accusation, a segregated Oscar ceremony, a Moroccan city destroyed and rebuilt from nothing, a pandemic's American arrival.

When February 29 comes, something happens.
